cur:catacombs-sarcophagus-31535.summary: A married couple is portrayed in the central shell; around them, on two levels, crowds of small figures enact biblical scenes, including Christ raising Lazarus from an aedicula-tomb. The sarcophagus shows how Roman workshops multiplied the same repertoire of saving miracles for Christian families of the 4th century.
facts: Commons records its provenance as the cemetery of San Callisto on the Via Appia.
A separate Commons photograph details its raising of Lazarus.

cur:manuscripts-petershausen-sacramentar.summary: Within a medallion framed by a gold scale pattern, Christ sits frontally on a cushioned throne against a blue ground, blessing and holding an open book on his knee. On the facing page Ecclesia, the personified Church, sits enthroned in a matching medallion; together they open the sacramentary proper.
facts: German Wikipedia notes that the double page of the enthroned Ecclesia and the enthroned Christ, like the Majestas of the Gero Codex, derives from the Lorsch Gospels.
The sacramentary was made around 980 at Reichenau for solemn services, probably by the scribe Anno of the Gero Codex, and reached the abbey of Petershausen only later, probably after a fire of 1159.
cur:manuscripts-petershausen-sacramentar.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-sixth-seal.summary: In a red medallion inscribed 'Thronus', the haloed Lord sits on a throne, blessing and holding a book, between angels labelled cherubim and seraphim, with elders standing at the sides. Below, the sun is darkened and the moon turns to blood, as the Latin captions say, and people hide in caves and among the trees from the face of him who sits on the throne.
facts: The Morgan Beatus is the work of the painter-scribe Magius (Maius), who is named in a colophon on fol. 293; it is one of the earliest works of the revived Spanish Apocalypse tradition and of so-called Mozarabic art.
The manuscript has 300 leaves of fine parchment and contains, besides Beatus's Commentary, Jerome's Commentary on Daniel.
cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-sixth-seal.notes: The enthroned figure has a plain halo; in the Beatus tradition the one on the throne is generally read as Christ (compare the Girona Beatus version, where he has a cross-nimbus).

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Against a purple ground, a haloed Christ turns away as men with swords and stones and a soldier in mail rush at him. The verse above asks the Lord to 'consider mine enemies; for they are many; and they hate me with cruel hatred'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The haloed victim is identified as Christ following the manuscript's Christological reading of the psalms.

cur:objects-bm-ezekiel-anastasis-ivory.summary: At the right, Christ appears in a great circular glory, enthroned on a footstool and holding an inscribed tablet, with a host of angels behind him. At the left a haloed figure, identified as the prophet Ezekiel, stands before a city wall and stretches out his hand, while small figures rise from the ground below — the dry bones coming to life. The panel links Ezekiel's vision of the resurrection of the dead with Christ's victory over death.
facts: The British Museum describes the subject as 'the Descent of Our Lord into Hell (Anastasis; Vision of Ezekiel)' and dates the panel to about 900–1000.
cur:objects-bm-ezekiel-anastasis-ivory.notes: The precise subject is debated; the museum title combines the Anastasis and the Vision of Ezekiel. Christ's presence in the glory is clear, but the reading of the left-hand figure follows the museum's interpretation.

cur:objects-coin-justinian-ii-first-reig.summary: On the obverse a majestic, bearded Christ with long hair looks straight out, raising his right hand in blessing and holding the Gospels, with a cross behind his head; the legend calls him IhS CRISTOS REX REGNANTIUM, 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. On the reverse the emperor stands holding a cross on steps, styled 'servant of Christ'. With this issue the image of Christ appeared for the first time on a coin, carrying the face of the Lord into the hands of everyone in the empire.
facts: Wikipedia notes that Justinian II was the first emperor to include the image of Christ on coinage issued in his name, moving the emperor's portrait to the reverse.

According to Wikipedia's article on Byzantine coinage, this innovation prompted the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik to abandon figural imitations of Byzantine coins and create a purely epigraphic Islamic coinage.

The obverse legend names Christ 'Rex regnantium' and the reverse styles Justinian 'servus Christi', servant of Christ, expressing the emperor's subordination to the heavenly King (legend as recorded for this specimen).
cur:objects-coin-justinian-ii-first-reig.notes: The second-reign type, with a different, curly-haired Christ, is already in the collection (Cleveland Museum of Art 2012.47; featured key 'solidus-of-justinian-ii-christ').

europeana:2021648/resource_document_coll.summary: This copper cross has four flaring arms with moulded ends, set on a short stepped shaft. The photograph shows the reverse, where a small mosaic panel on a blue ground carries the Chi-Rho monogram of Christ with the letters alpha and omega. According to Castle Huis Bergh, the front holds a matching, very fine mosaic of the head of Christ, so the cross would have carried both his name and his face in procession.
facts: The castle's catalogue describes the cross as shaped like a St Andrew's cross, a square with deeply scooped sides whose corners end in feet, standing on a short heavy shaft.
It notes that a small piece of the mosaic beside the head of Christ is missing.
europeana:2021648/resource_document_coll.notes: Identification uncertain: the head of Christ is described by the museum but is on the side not shown in the image, which shows only the Chi-Rho. The 6th–7th-century date comes from the museum record and could not be independently verified; micromosaic decoration on such a cross is unusual, and the date should be treated with caution.
